articles.title: Comment: Europe’s greenwashing paradox – could SFDR undermine EmpCo enforcement? - Responsible Investor
articles.summary: Comment: Europe’s greenwashing paradox – could SFDR undermine EmpCo enforcement?  Responsible Investor
articles.full_text:
Since 27 September, tougher EU consumer-protection rules have been in force against greenwashing under the Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive (EmpCo).
They restrict generic environmental claims, discipline claims about future environmental performance, and subject sustainability labels to tighter controls.
At the same time, Brussels is revising its Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) and creating fund categories that could give some weak sustainability claims greater authority – and make them harder to challenge.
EmpCo’s logic is straightforward: a green claim is not limited to an explicit promise. It may be conveyed by a label, product name, image, colour scheme or overall presentation – and must not mislead the average consumer.
Claims about future environmental performance require clear, objective, publicly available and verifiable commitments and targets, set out in a realistic implementation plan with measurable, time-bound targets and regular independent verification.
EmpCo also bars sustainability labels unless they are based on a certification scheme or established by a public authority.
The SFDR revision would create product categories rather than labels. But those statutory sustainability categories will function as labels in the market: public designations that private fund managers use to identify and market products.
Official categories create legitimate expectations among investors, advisers and fund selectors, and invite reliance on regulatory recognition as a substitute for scrutiny. That makes their design decisive.
European policymakers are now seeking to streamline disclosures and replace the de facto Article 8 and 9 labels with official Sustainable, Transition and ESG Basics categories backed by formal criteria: minimum investment thresholds, exclusions and specified qualifying investment routes. The proposal presents them as tools for mobilising and allocating capital towards the transition of the real economy.
“Claims about future environmental performance require clear, objective, publicly available and verifiable commitments and targets”
That makes the regulation’s interaction with EmpCo consequential. Under Article 3(4) of the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD), which EmpCo amends, sector-specific EU rules prevail in the event of conflict, but only for the aspects they specifically regulate.
The European Commission’s SFDR explanatory memorandum and recital 12 expressly state that proper compliance with SFDR requirements should satisfy the corresponding UCPD consumer-protection requirements for sustainability claims within its scope.
Consumer authorities may still challenge product language that goes beyond what the rules authorise. The extent of protection will depend on how specifically the final SFDR defines a category’s meaning and permitted use.
SFDR’s greenwashing risk
If SFDR categories themselves are weak, EmpCo may be left policing the wording around official designations while their compliant use becomes harder to challenge.
That makes it all the more important to address greenwashing risk within SFDR at two levels: the credibility of the categories and the coherence of the products that use them. Neither requires reopening the architecture of the proposed regime.
The first requirement is credible categories. Formal criteria are indispensable. They provide legal certainty, comparability and observable conditions for supervision. Where those criteria remain under negotiation, they must be compatible with what category names reasonably lead investors to expect.
Consider the proposed Transition category. Under a political compromise, it could include investment in some companies developing new fossil-fuel projects if they meet certain conditions, including Taxonomy-aligned capital expenditure.
But “Transition” is likely to signal something different to a retail investor: a business moving away from fossil-fuel dependence, rather than one diversifying into clean energy while also expanding oil-and-gas supply.
“A framework intended to curb misleading sustainability claims may end up greenlighting greenwashing”
The second requirement is coherent products. Even well-designed criteria have limits. They are gatekeepers, not proof that a product coherently serves the purpose its category conveys or can plausibly contribute to the outcome it implies.
Products built around portfolio-emissions compression illustrate the point. A fund can lower weighted-average carbon metrics simply by reallocating away from carbon-intensive holdings, regardless of their issuers’ importance to the transition, their transition performance or actual decarbonisation.
That may improve the fund’s reported carbon footprint, and possibly reduce its exposure to carbon-price risk. But that alone does not show that the strategy finances the transformation of industrial sectors, rewards companies’ transition efforts, or supports decarbonisation progress.
This is not a thought experiment. Portfolio-level emissions reduction is a qualifying investment approach in the proposed SFDR revision, and underpins the EU’s official climate-benchmark standards, the use of which receives preferential treatment under the proposal.
The answer is not to prescribe one investment model. Funds may support the transition by financing specific projects or assets, investing in bonds or loans with proceeds earmarked for transition or enabling activities, allocating capital to companies making credible progress, or using stewardship and engagement to press for change. But flexibility must be matched by accountability.
Alongside formal qualification criteria, managers using an official category should have to show their work: explain and evidence, in standardised form, how the objective they pursue serves the category’s purpose; how their strategy and implementation are expected to achieve it; why their indicators are informative; and, where real-economy effects are claimed or implied, why those effects are plausible.
This would not guarantee a climate outcome, alter eligibility or exclude products that meet the formal criteria. It would add substantiation, not another investment model or eligibility test. It would give investors, advisers and fund selectors the evidence needed to distinguish credible strategies from weaker ones – and regulators a firmer basis for supervision.
ESMA’s 12 October notes on transition and impact claims point in this direction. They call for explanations linking ambitions, strategies, metrics and results, and warn against equating portfolio decarbonisation with real-economy emissions reductions or confusing investee impact with investor impact.
These notes address non-regulatory communications and create no new requirements. Their logic should inform SFDR’s statutory product requirements, including substantiation of the claims conveyed by the categories themselves.
The broader lesson is that public categories do not merely discipline private claims; they can also legitimise and shield them. When weakly designed, they give questionable claims a stronger regulatory footing. A claim may not become less misleading, but it can become more trusted, less scrutinised and harder to challenge.
As EU lawmakers finalise the rules, they should align category criteria more closely with their stated purposes and require fund managers to substantiate how their investment processes serve them. Otherwise, a framework intended to curb misleading sustainability claims may end up greenlighting greenwashing.
Frédéric Ducoulombier is programme director, climate regulation and policies, at EDHEC Climate Institute.

articles.summary:
Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has issued rules aligning listed companies’ sustainability disclosures with International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) standards. Companies on the Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) in […]
The post Thailand’s SEC Orders SET50 Companies to Report Under ISSB Standards From 2027 appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Thailand’s SEC Orders SET50 Companies to Report Under ISSB Standards From 2027
- SET50 first: Companies in the SET50 Index at the December 2026 review must report 2027 data under the new rules.
- Five transition reliefs: Relief covers comparative climate data, reporting timeframes, GHG calculation standards and Scope 3 emissions.
- Assurance required: Greenhouse gas disclosures must be verified by assurance providers under internationally accepted standards.
Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has issued rules aligning listed companies’ sustainability disclosures with International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) standards. Companies on the Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) in the SET50 Index at the December 2026 review must report first, for 2027. Nine related notifications have been in effect since 26 October 2026.
The SEC revised its reporting forms and registration statements to align with the ISSB’s IFRS S1 and IFRS S2. SET100 constituents at the December 2027 review follow, reporting for 2028. The rules will later extend to all SET and Market for Alternative Investment (mai) companies. Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs), infrastructure funds, infrastructure trusts and property funds will also be covered in later phases.
To help companies build data systems, the SEC set five transition reliefs. These include exemption from comparative climate data in the first reporting year and flexibility in the reporting timeframe. Companies may also use equivalent greenhouse gas (GHG) calculation standards and skip Scope 3, or value-chain, emissions at first. Meanwhile, GHG disclosures must be verified by assurance providers under internationally accepted standards, so investors can rely on them.
RELATED ARTICLE: Thailand SEC Updates ‘ESG Product Platform’ with Key SRI Fund Data to Boost Sustainable Investing
The SEC also published Form 56-1 One Report-S, its annual registration statement and annual report form. It has run training programs for the private sector since 2024 and says it will continue them. Its disclosure manuals were prepared with domestic and international strategic partners. The SEC did not disclose penalties for non-compliance or reporting years for the phases after SET100.
Who It Affects
- SET50 companies: Must report 2027 sustainability and climate data under IFRS S1 and S2, with assured GHG figures.
- SET100 companies: Must start reporting for 2028 if they are constituents at the December 2027 review.
- Other listed companies and trusts: All SET and mai companies, REITs, infrastructure funds and trusts, and property funds join in later phases.
- Assurance providers: Must verify listed companies’ GHG disclosures against internationally accepted assurance standards.

articles.title: The climate cost of a loose ETS cap - Carbon Market Watch
articles.summary: The climate cost of a loose ETS cap  Carbon Market Watch
articles.full_text:
In the difficult negotiation process surrounding the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), one of the most contentious points for member states and Members of the European Parliament is determining whether or not the recently proposed ETS revision will enable the EU to reach its established emission reduction goals. Research from Öko-Institut and Climact suggests this aim will not be reached: the carbon market risks being flooded with allowances, while decarbonisation efforts are unloaded onto non-ETS sectors.
European Union member states will now be allowed to rely on international carbon credits to meet their 2040 climate targets. While the bloc’s flagship target remains a 90% net emissions reduction compared to 1990, a March 2026 amendment to the European Climate Law allows capitals to limit domestic cuts to 85% and cover the remaining balance of up to 5% through international carbon credits.
During the ongoing revision of the EU’s flagship climate policy, understanding the implications of the Emissions Trading System 1 (EU ETS1) for the European reduction targets is key to determining how targets for non-ETS1 sectors should be set. Yet, progress on emissions reductions will occur at two different speeds. In 2005, domestic emissions under the EU ETS1 accounted for around 50% of the EU-27’s total net emissions. In 2024, that dropped to 38%, a 50% reduction since 2005, while sectors covered by the Effort Sharing Regulation (ESR) have achieved a less impressive 20% reduction since the same year.
Modelling from Climact estimates that the Commission’s 17 July proposal to revise the ETS might under-deliver towards the EU’s domestic climate target and that significant effort would pass to non-ETS sectors, such as agriculture.
Climact’s simulator puts the ETS1’s own domestic reduction at around 81% against a 2005 baseline, which would require ESR sectors to reach close to a 78% domestic reduction over the same period to keep track with the economy-wide target of 85%. However, this scenario relies on millions of international credits, from a market that is currently not delivering its promises.
A scenario where international credits contribute to 2% of the reduction would require an ESR target to climb substantially to 83%, a rate even more ambitious than the ETS sectors. Climact estimates that such a steep ESR target is unrealistic. ESR sectors achieved reductions of only 20% between 2005 and 2024: this means that to adapt to the current ETS proposal, ESR sectors would need to slash emissions by a factor of four times faster than in the past, relative to the previous 20 years since the ETS commenced operation.
What is the cap capping?
The Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) is a cap-and-trade system that aims to limit emissions of the power, industrial, aviation and maritime sectors. The cap sets an annual limit on the supply of new pollution permits that installations covered by the system will need to cover their emissions. The emission reduction target is achieved by a constant decrease in this cap. The cap decreases linearly, following the so-called Linear Reduction Factor (LRF), which is expressed as a percentage of the 2013 total cap.
The LRF has changed significantly since the system began. From 2013 to 2020, the LRF was set at 1.74% (around 34 million carbon permits per year), then at 2.2% as of 2021, 4.3% from 2024 to 2027, and 4.4% from 2028 to 2030. A small change to the LRF significantly impacts the amount of emissions allowed in the system. 
CMW analysis shows that since 2013, emissions of the industry, power and maritime sectors have never exceeded 86% of the cap. This leads to a question: what exactly is the cap capping?
Rather than tightening the cap to absorb this surplus, the Commission’s new proposal tilts in the opposite direction, attempting to loosen the cap even further by substantially reducing the LRF. The proposed LRF is set at 3.7% for the period 2031–2035 and flattens to 1.7% from 2036 onwards, setting the LRF at a lower rate than it was more than a decade before.
Based on CMW calculations, this retrograde action alone will add two billion metric tonnes of CO2 to the allowable emissions under the cap for the power, industrial and maritime sectors, representing an additional 67% of the allowable emissions following the current trend and stretching the cap until 2048. However, when accounting for the combination of the different features proposed by the Commission (see below for more details), Climact estimated an additional 2.2 billion allowances compared to the status quo.
The proposal incorporates the planned purchase of 260 million international credits starting in 2036, reducing the European domestic abatement requirement in 2040 from 90% to 85%.
But the LRF change is not the only mechanism that increases the ETS1 carbon budget in the Commission’s proposal. The indirect integration of domestic carbon dioxide removals (CDR) into the system will further inflate the emittable tonnes of CO2, to fund permanent CDR projects. These emissions come on top of the cap, ballooning the overall carbon budget by another 250 million allowances from 2031 to 2040. This represents an additional 7% increase from the current trend.
Additionally, the ETS1 Market Stability Reserve (MSR1) is meant to be the system’s shock absorber, pulling allowances out of circulation when there’s oversupply and releasing them if the market were to eventually tighten. In April, the European Commission proposed substantially dismantling the core mechanism of MSR1: the invalidation clause which cancels allowances permanently when the Reserve breaches a set oversupply threshold. Although ongoing negotiations on this file indicate that the invalidation clause is highly likely to survive, a carbon bomb has been lit for the future that could still result in an additional 350 million allowances released on the market after 2035.
In combination, the weaker LRF, international credits, the inclusion of CDR and the carryover holdings in the MSR1 still don’t account for all potential sources of allowances, and therefore all the tonnes of CO2 that can possibly be emitted under the ETS system. There are millions of oversupplied allowances in circulation due to the system being structurally oversupplied in the past and present (the so-called TNAC, total number of allowances in circulation). And there is yet another pot of allowances that could reach the market in the next few years: the New Entrants Reserve (NER), put aside for new installation and new production capacity entering the ETS, sitting at over 300 million allowances according to the European Commission Carbon Market reports.
Extra room to pollute
Despite the uncertain outlook of the market due to the proposed rules, an independent assessment reached a similar conclusion: under the Commission’s proposal, the ETS would be significantly oversupplied by 2040, making it likely to miss the newly agreed climate target.
Öko-Institut estimates the entire oversupply over 2031-2040 at 1.9 billion EUAs, equivalent to 35% of total demand. Note that this doesn’t take the latest MSR1 negotiation outcomes into account, so it could potentially be about 350 million too high based on the progress of ongoing negotiations.
The supply-demand gap is significant enough for Öko-Institut to recommend that the LRF remain at 4.4% until at least 2035. This recommendation was also raised by Agora Energiewende, stressing that maintaining the current LRF trajectory until 2035 is crucial to create stability and investment certainty.
The lesson learned from the past two decades of the scheme is not that it needs more flexibility, but that the flexibility that has been accumulated for years with banked surplus and allowances handed out for free goes against the system’s core objective. Adding a further two billion tonnes of headroom and extending the cap does not fix that problem, it multiplies it. The ETS needs to stay on its pre-proposal trajectory to rapidly limit the EU’s vulnerability to international fossil fuel markets (and the climate disasters those fossil fuels cause).
Room to pollute, room to fail
Taken together, these findings describe a single mechanism working at two dysfunctional levels. Inside the ETS1, a persistently loose cap blunts the price signal that’s supposed to drive industrial decarbonisation. Outside the ETS1, this leniency creates spillover pressure on the ESR sectors.
Twenty years into the EU ETS, the same evidence continually reappears: the system keeps handing out more room than the market needs. Emissions have never reached close to the cap since 2013, and independent modelling demonstrates that the Commission’s proposal would only stretch that slack further, oversupplying the market well into the 2040s and blunting the price signal the ETS depends on to drive decarbonisation.
The EU’s 2040 climate target is at risk. Every extra billion tonnes of headroom is a billion tonnes of decarbonisation the ETS won’t deliver, and that needs to be reduced from other polluting sectors.
However, EU policymakers now have the chance to not only keep the ETS on track, but to raise the standard for the bloc’s flagship climate policy. The LRF must remain at 4.4% through at least until 2035, avoiding any regression to levels seen more than a decade ago. The MSR’s absorption and cancellation functions must be maintained, not weakened. And crucially, carbon removals should be kept out of ETS to keep the carbon market laser-focused on emissions reduction.

articles.title: WMO Says CO2 Hit Record 426.8 ppm in 2025, Flags SF6 and Hydrogen Leaks
articles.summary:
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the UN weather agency, said greenhouse gas levels in the atmosphere hit record highs in 2025. Global average CO2 concentration reached 426.8 parts per million […]
The post WMO Says CO2 Hit Record 426.8 ppm in 2025, Flags SF6 and Hydrogen Leaks appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
WMO Says CO2 Hit Record 426.8 ppm in 2025, Flags SF6 and Hydrogen Leaks
- Record CO2 level: Global average atmospheric CO2 reached 426.8 parts per million in 2025, according to the WMO.
- Other gases at records: Methane and nitrous oxide also hit record highs, at 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels.
- El Nino outlook: The WMO expects CO2 concentrations to rise further this year as a powerful El Nino sets in.
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the UN weather agency, said greenhouse gas levels in the atmosphere hit record highs in 2025. Global average CO2 concentration reached 426.8 parts per million (ppm), about 153% of the 1750 pre-industrial level, according to its report released on Tuesday. The level rose by 2.8 ppm from the previous year. That was a bigger annual increase than the average over the past decade.
Methane and nitrous oxide, two other important greenhouse gases, stood at 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. However, the WMO noted that the report measures the amount of gas that accumulates in the atmosphere, not new annual emissions.
El Nino Outlook
The WMO expects CO2 concentrations to rise further this year because of fossil fuel burning and the onset of a powerful El Nino. The agency said El Nino will cause drier weather and make it harder for carbon sinks to absorb emissions. The WMO did not quantify the expected increase for this year or detail its measurement methodology.
Meanwhile, parts of the world, including Europe, saw scorching summer temperatures this year, while Asia and other regions were hit by devastating floods. “Every additional part per million matters because it traps additional heat. In effect, we are supercharging the ocean and the atmosphere,” said Ko Barrett, WMO Deputy Secretary-General. “That means that heatwaves, tropical cyclones, and rainstorms are intensifying faster than our historical baselines prepared us for.”
SF6 and Hydrogen Risks
The WMO said the 2025 increase in sulfur hexafluoride (SF6), a greenhouse gas widely used in electrical equipment, was a record high. Hydrogen concentrations also rose 5.3% between 2010 and 2024, the agency added. As a result, the WMO said hydrogen leakage and the long persistence of SF6 could undermine some climate benefits of the global energy transition. “The energy transition is essential and welcome, but as with every transition, it has to be done in a smart way and informed by environmental observations,” Barrett said.
RELATED ARTICLE: WMO European State of the Climate Report Reveals Europe Logged Warmest Year Ever in 2024
Who It Affects
- COP31 negotiators: The WMO will share the findings with negotiators at the COP31 UN climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, in November.
- Electrical equipment users: SF6 has a global warming potential, or heat-trapping power, more than 24,000 times that of CO2, and can remain in the atmosphere for more than 1,000 years.
- Hydrogen producers and operators: Leaks from infrastructure used to produce, transport and store hydrogen can affect atmospheric chemistry and indirectly add to warming, the WMO said, although hydrogen itself is not a greenhouse gas.

articles.title: India Sizes $220 Billion Three-Year Need for Solar, Storage, Hydrogen and Grids
articles.summary:
India needs about $220 billion in clean energy investment over the next three years, a senior government official said on Wednesday. The money would help the country reach 500 GW […]
The post India Sizes $220 Billion Three-Year Need for Solar, Storage, Hydrogen and Grids appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
India Sizes $220 Billion Three-Year Need for Solar, Storage, Hydrogen and Grids
- Investment need: India needs about $220 billion in clean energy investment over the next three years.
- Capacity target: Non-fossil power capacity stands at about 308 GW, against a 500 GW goal for 2030.
- Uncontracted projects: About 40 GW of clean energy projects awarded in recent tenders have yet to find customers.
India needs about $220 billion in clean energy investment over the next three years, a senior government official said on Wednesday. The money would help the country reach 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030. Santosh Kumar Sarangi is the top official at the federal clean energy ministry. He said the investment is needed in solar and wind power, battery energy storage, green hydrogen and transmission infrastructure.
India currently has about 308 GW of non-fossil fuel power generation capacity. The 500 GW goal is part of broader efforts to reach net-zero emissions by 2070. Between 2024 and 2026, the sector attracted about $64 billion of private investment, including $6.2 billion from foreign investors. The government invested an additional $6 billion over the same period, Sarangi said.
India has awarded a large number of clean energy project tenders in recent years, alongside an increased clean energy push. As a result, about 40 GW of clean energy projects have yet to find customers. The official did not disclose how the $220 billion would be split between public and private sources or across technologies.
India has also developed a market for about 550,000 tonnes of green ammonia demand from overseas buyers, including Japan and South Korea, Sarangi said. Green ammonia is made using hydrogen produced with renewable power.
RELATED ARTICLE: India’s New ESG Rules to Address Corporate Green Washing
Who It Affects
- State governments: The federal government is working with states to encourage them to take on clean power and ramp up battery storage, Sarangi said.
- Foreign investors and pension funds: Indian officials will meet investors next week at a clean energy summit in New Delhi. Talks will cover potential investments from several countries, including pension funds from Canada.

articles.title: DuPont Commits to 83% Scope 1 and 2 Emissions Cut by 2035 as SBTi Validates Net-Zero Plan
articles.summary:
DuPont said the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) has validated its net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets. The core commitment is an 83% cut in absolute Scope 1 and […]
The post DuPont Commits to 83% Scope 1 and 2 Emissions Cut by 2035 as SBTi Validates Net-Zero Plan appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
DuPont Commits to 83% Scope 1 and 2 Emissions Cut by 2035 as SBTi Validates Net-Zero Plan
- Near-term targets: DuPont commits to cut absolute Scope 1 and 2 emissions 83% and Scope 3 emissions 63% by 2035.
- Net-zero goal: The company targets net-zero value-chain emissions by 2050, with 90% absolute cuts across all three scopes.
- Progress to date: By 2025, DuPont had cut combined Scope 1 and 2 emissions 76% and Scope 3 emissions 59%.
DuPont said the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) has validated its net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets. The core commitment is an 83% cut in absolute Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2035, from 2019 levels. Scope 1 and 2 cover direct emissions and purchased energy. The validation covers both near- and long-term targets, including net zero across DuPont’s value chain by 2050.
DuPont also commits to cut absolute Scope 3 emissions 63% by 2035 from a 2020 base year. Scope 3 covers indirect emissions across its value chain. By 2050, it targets 90% absolute cuts in all three scopes, using the same base years. The company did not disclose the investment, delivery plan or absolute emissions volumes behind these percentages.
SBTi is a corporate climate action organization that develops standards, tools and guidance for setting emissions reduction targets. Those targets are designed to match what is needed to reach net zero by 2050. DuPont said the validation shows its climate commitment while supporting customers cutting emissions in their own value chains. “SBTi validation reinforces the rigor we place on our climate commitments and the progress we’re making to reduce emissions across our operations and value chain,” said Scott Collick, Chief Sustainability Officer at DuPont. “By advancing sustainable innovation, building more resilient operations and collaborating across our value chain, we can reduce our footprint while helping our customers advance their sustainability goals.”
RELATED ARTICLE: DuPont Sustainable Solutions Unveils New Brand Name: dss+
What’s New
The new goals are DuPont’s second set of near-term SBTi climate targets. They follow its previous SBTi-validated 2030 emissions reduction target, which the company achieved ahead of schedule. DuPont has already moved most of the way: in 2025, combined Scope 1 and 2 emissions were 76% below 2019. Meanwhile, Scope 3 emissions were 59% below the 2020 baseline.
Why It Matters
SBTi validation gives DuPont externally checked targets for its next decade of emissions cuts. Based on 2025 progress, it needs 7 more percentage points on Scope 1 and 2 and 4 on Scope 3. That positions DuPont to win supply contracts with customers cutting their own value-chain emissions, if Scope 3 cuts stay on track.

articles.title: Trawling in protected areas: the legal battle reaches Italy - Materia Rinnovabile | Renewable Matter
articles.summary: Trawling in protected areas: the legal battle reaches Italy  Materia Rinnovabile | Renewable Matter
articles.full_text:
On a map, the waters of the Tyrrhenian Sea off Tuscany and of the Ionian Sea off Apulia are designated under Natura 2000, the EU network meant to protect vulnerable habitats and species. Underwater, however, trawl nets are still dragged across the seabed, causing profound environmental impacts. In September, ClientEarth and Legambiente, supported by Blue Marine Foundation, decided to take action against the Italian authorities over these two marine protected areas (MPAs), asking them to enforce the EU Habitats Directive by assessing the impacts of bottom trawling and, where needed, restricting it. The move is part of a broader European strategy to defend MPAs in court, pursued by the MPA Legal Coalition: eleven organisations, including ClientEarth, Environmental Justice Foundation, Oceana, Seas At Risk and Blue Marine, that connect national legal actions to a coordinated effort at the European level.
Italian government data shows that MPAs cover around 11% of the country's waters. However, a Greenpeace analysis found that only less than 1% is effectively protected, a long way from the 30% target for 2030. The first site, Tutela del Tursiops Truncatus, covers roughly 374,000 hectares off Tuscany within the Pelagos Sanctuary, the cross-border marine mammal reserve shared by France, Italy and Monaco and one of the largest MPAs in Europe. The area was designated as a refuge for bottlenose dolphins, yet the NGOs call it a "paper park" because bottom trawling is generally still allowed.
The second, Litorale di Gallipoli-Isola di Sant'Andrea, is in Apulia and hosts seagrass meadows and reefs. Much of it has never been mapped, and trawlers continue to work in it. Remarkably, about a third of the Mediterranean's bottom trawlers sail under the Italian flag, according to ClientEarth, putting heavy pressure on fish populations and marine habitats.
"These two sites were chosen because they share the same weaknesses and issues," underlines Francesco Maletto, Ocean Lawyer at ClientEarth. "Both MPAs were designated for Posidonia meadows and coralligenous habitats, but in both bottom trawling takes place and they lack the mapping needed to manage them. The Tuscan site is also much smaller than the Pelagos Sanctuary, a cross-border conservation area with scarce regulation and inadequate enforcement."
The gap between protection on paper and in practice
The legal claim brought forward by ClientEarth and Legambiente does not call for new legislation, but for the effective enforcement of the existing one. "The rules are set and they are ambitious. We do not need to change them; we need to apply them and make them work," explains Maletto, who points to an enforcement gap: the distance between protection on paper and protection in practice.
The legal basis is Article 6 of the EU Habitats Directive. Under it, authorities must prevent the deterioration of designated habitats, and any activity that could affect a site may go ahead only after its impact has been assessed and proven harmless. In Italy, that assessment is known as VIncA (Valutazione di Incidenza). "Trawling takes place in these areas indiscriminately, without any evaluation of its impacts," says Maletto. "That assessment is mandatory, yet it is not being done for fishing. These are obligations already in force in our legal system, but politics often lacks adequate enforcement to respect them." Maletto points out a distinction between Natura 2000 sites and Italy's national MPAs. Trawling is already banned in the latter, so the problem does not arise there. The issue lies in the Natura 2000 sites, where the measures needed to protect habitats, such as bans and zoning, have not been put in place.
From administrative requests to the Lake Vico precedent
The Italian case is still at an early stage, since the organisations have not yet gone to court. They have submitted administrative requests asking the competent regional authorities to take the necessary measures to protect the two sites. "If the authorities act on this request, we get real change without needing to go to court," John Condon, Lead Lawyer of the Marine Ecosystems team at ClientEarth, explains to Renewable Matter. "If they do not, we will consider whether it is necessary to escalate the matter to the Administrative Court to bring about real change."
The Habitats Directive obliges authorities to take actual measures to prevent habitat damage, whether they act on their own or are later ordered to by a court. This law is built to require action, and the Italian case offers a precedent. In 2024, ClientEarth won a landmark ruling from the Council of State on Lake Vico, which for the first time recognised that this part of the Habitats Directive can be directly enforced. Condon adds that "the court ordered the Lazio region to take real corrective steps within six months, and the ruling could not be appealed". A similar outcome for the two marine sites, he points out, "could mean the authorities are legally required to take meaningful action in the water, such as mapping the seabed, assessing the risks of bottom trawling on the protected area, and putting in place real protective measures, possibly including trawling restrictions".
A legal strategy on a European scale
The Italian case is part of a broader scenario, with litigation over bottom trawling in protected areas now under way in France, Spain, the Netherlands and Germany. In May, the District Court of The Hague ruled that Dutch trawlers could no longer fish in the Dogger Bank protected area without a permit and an environmental assessment. Linking these efforts is what the MPA Legal Coalition was created for, and according to Condon, it adds value in three ways. The first is coordination, because, instead of proceeding in isolation, national actions converge into a broader European strategy.
The second is a shared evidence base. Members from different NGOs exchange legal analysis, scientific evidence and lessons from their own cases, which is important because EU law requires decisions affecting protected sites to rest on the best available science. And yet, Condon points out, "destructive activities such as bottom trawling continue to be authorised in marine protected areas despite extensive evidence" of their potential impacts.
The third is pressure on the European Commission. Coalition members have filed two complaints covering six Member States: Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Spain. They ask Brussels to ensure compliance with the Habitats Directive and to use its enforcement powers where necessary.
National cases and Commission complaints, Condon explains, are "closely connected, but they serve different and complementary purposes". National cases like the Italian one are tied to specific sites, yet their implications can reach further, because the obligations stem from common EU law, and a ruling in one country can set a precedent for others. The complaints to the Commission work at a different level. They target systemic non-compliance, and the sites they cite serve as "representative examples" of wider failures. If Brussels opens infringement proceedings, a Member State can be required to bring its entire governance framework into line with EU law, not just the single area at issue.
The 30% by 2030 target
The EU has pledged to protect 30% of its seas by 2030, but the Coalition argues that areas which exist only on a map should not count towards that goal. Legambiente has made a similar call, asking for the ban of bottom trawling in MPAs by 2030, in line with the EU's 2023 fisheries action plan.
For both Maletto and Condon, the rules are already written and what is missing is their application, and courts are only one way to get there. "Our approach is constructive; litigation is an important tool, but it has to drive good policy," Condon concludes. "We engage very closely with policymakers in Brussels and across Europe by providing clear and pragmatic policy recommendations to ensure that MPAs work both for the environment and coastal communities. Acting collectively enables us to demonstrate that shortcomings in MPA management are not isolated national problems but reflect wider implementation and enforcement gaps across Europe."

articles.full_text:
EU proposes climate resilience law with 3°C planning trajectory
The European Commission has proposed a European Climate Resilience Law as part of a wider EU Framework for Climate Resilience, presented on 27 October.
The draft regulation sets a common reference trajectory of 1.5°C of warming by 2030, 2°C by 2050 and 3°C by 2100.
Member states would encourage public authorities to consider it in budgeting, spatial planning and environmental impact assessments (EIAs).
Each member state would complete a national climate risk assessment by 2029 and adopt a national strategic resilience plan by the end of 2030, both reviewed every five years.
The Commission estimates EU adaptation and resilience investment needs at about $79bn (€70bn) a year.
The proposal now goes to the Parliament and Council.
ISSB consults on nature-related disclosures
The International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) has opened a consultation on proposals for nature-related disclosures, launched during COP17.
The exposure draft proposes a practice statement on how companies should disclose nature-related risks and opportunities that arise from their dependencies and impacts on nature.
The proposals draw extensively on the work of the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures. The TNFD has completed its own technical work and will continue to support the ISSB, it says.
Comments can be submitted via an online survey until 19 February.
UN finds national climate plans substantially off track
The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) has published its 2026 assessment of nationally determined contributions (NDCs), ahead of COP31.
The report covers 127 new NDCs from 154 parties, representing about 71% of global emissions in 2019.
Implemented in full, they would bring 2035 emissions to an average of 6% below 2019 levels, or about 9% if conditional elements are delivered, it says.
The report says collective progress is "substantially off track" from the reductions required by the science, with best-estimate warming of 1.7°C to 2.3°C by the end of the century.
Of the parties covered, 86% included an adaptation component and 94% plan to or may use voluntary cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.
US EPA launches PFAS technology strategy
The US EPA has launched PFAS TECH, its first agency-wide strategy for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) treatment and destruction technologies.
The strategy has three goals:
- accelerating research into treatment and destruction methods, such as foam fractionation and supercritical water oxidation;
- running pilot projects at Superfund sites, military facilities, wastewater treatment plants and drinking water systems; and
- practical support, including guidance, a Break the Bond Navigator tool and help for water systems to access funding.
The EPA intends to give research grants for PFAS destruction through its Science to Achieve Results (STAR) and Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) programmes.
US and EU loosen methane rules
The US EPA has proposed revisions to its 2024 rules for oil and natural gas operations under the Clean Air Act.
The proposal would rescind the super emitter programme and restore 95% efficient flaring as the standard for associated gas, rather than requiring that gas to be routed to a sales line.
The EPA estimates the changes would save about $45bn.
In the EU, the European Parliament voted on 22 October for a three-year postponement of certain obligations under the EU Methane Regulation, rejecting the Commission’s proposed one-year delay.
The rules require fossil fuel importers to show that non-EU suppliers meet equivalent monitoring, reporting and verification standards.
ERM report finds experts want sustainability agenda overhaul
Fifty-nine per cent of more than 600 sustainability experts across 57 countries want the sustainability agenda radically revised – and 95% support some form of change, research by ERM, Globescan and Volans has revealed.
Only 5% strongly believe companies will meet their 2030 climate commitments, while 70% see deeper integration within businesses as a critical route to better outcomes.
EPA claims $1.6tn in deregulatory savings
The US EPA said deregulatory actions – finalised between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026 – will save more than $1.6tn, mostly from rescinding the 2009 Endangerment Finding and repealing most power plant greenhouse gas requirements.
It also pointed to proposed National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) procedures that would cut a typical environmental review from four years to two.

Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has issued rules aligning listed companies’ sustainability disclosures with International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) standards. Companies on the Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) in the SET50 Index at the December 2026 review must report first, for 2027. Nine related notifications have been in effect since 26 October 2026.

The rules will later extend to all SET and Market for Alternative Investment (mai) companies. Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs), infrastructure funds, infrastructure trusts and property funds will also be covered in later phases.
To help companies build data systems, the SEC set five transition reliefs. These include exemption from comparative climate data in the first reporting year and flexibility in the reporting timeframe. Companies may also use equivalent greenhouse gas (GHG) calculation standards and skip Scope 3, or value-chain, emissions at first. Meanwhile, GHG disclosures must be verified by assurance providers under internationally accepted standards, so investors can rely on them.

articles.title: 5 actions governments must take to address modern slavery in climate solutions - Walk Free
articles.summary: 5 actions governments must take to address modern slavery in climate solutions  Walk Free
articles.full_text:
You can search the content of this website using the search box below.
Governments must address modern slavery risks in climate solutions at the 2026 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), taking place in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9–20 November.
The transition to a carbon-free economy is creating new human rights challenges. These include forced labour in renewable energy and critical mineral supply chains, as well as the heightened vulnerability to exploitation of people displaced by climate-related disasters.
There are 5 key actions to prevent modern slavery and make sure the transition to a carbon-free economy protects workers and communities.
Women and girls, Indigenous Peoples, and communities experiencing food insecurity face greater risks of exploitation when climate change threatens their homes and access to essential resources. Losing traditional lands and livelihoods also increases the risk of forced migration.
Governments must embed human rights protections into climate policies and programs, and ensure people with lived experience of climate impacts and exploitation have a meaningful role in shaping these policies.
The shift away from fossil fuels and towards renewable energy must deliver decent work and protect workers from exploitation.
Workers experience forced labour in renewable energy and critical mineral supply chains, from mineral extraction to manufacturing.
Governments must address and prevent forced labour in these supply chains through strong human rights due diligence laws.
They must also support workers and communities affected by the phase-out of fossil fuel industries, ensuring the transition delivers fair employment opportunities and respects workers’ rights.
Governments must engage with businesses, investors, workers, civil society, and survivor leaders to raise awareness of modern slavery risks and strengthen accountability across supply chains.
Clear guidance on human rights due diligence and disclosure obligations is essential to help businesses understand their responsibilities and take action to prevent forced labour.
Sourcing these minerals from regions with higher forced labour risks presents serious human rights challenges.
Governments must support ethical sourcing and diversify supply chains to reduce dependence on high-risk resources. They should also promote the use of sustainable technologies that reduce demand for critical minerals.
Climate-related disasters and environmental degradation force people from their homes and threaten their livelihoods.
People displaced by climate change may struggle to find stable work, increasing their vulnerability to exploitation and forced labour.
Governments must help affected communities rebuild their livelihoods and access social protection. People who lose their traditional sources of income need viable alternatives to reduce their risk of exploitation.
COP31 presents an opportunity for governments to strengthen human rights protections in climate policies and ensure the transition to a carbon-free economy delivers decent work and justice for all.
These protections must be put into practice across climate policies, renewable energy supply chains, and responses to climate displacement. Climate action must not come at the cost of the people it is meant to protect.

articles.full_text:
Green Climate Fund Approves $140 Million for Green Hydrogen in South Africa and Namibia
- GCF approval: The Green Climate Fund approved $140 million for Climate Investor Three.
- Country split: SA-H2 Fund gets $84 million and SDG Namibia One $56 million.
- Fundraising target: CI3 is raising capital towards a $1.2 billion target.
The Green Climate Fund (GCF) has approved $140 million in catalytic financing for blended finance investment manager Climate Fund Managers. The money backs Climate Investor Three (CI3), its global industrial decarbonisation facility, including green hydrogen in Southern Africa. GCF approved it at its 46th Board meeting in Songdo, Republic of Korea, on 26-29 October 2026.
CI3 invests through SA-H2 Fund (SA-H2) in South Africa and SDG Namibia One Fund (SDG Namibia One) in Namibia. $84 million goes to SA-H2’s Construction Equity Tranche, which funds projects through construction. SDG Namibia One receives USD 56 million: $15 million for its Development Tranche, which funds early-stage work, and $41 million for construction equity.
The financing comes through GCF’s Southern African Industrial Decarbonisation Facility (SIDF). The Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) oversees SIDF as its Accredited Entity, reporting to GCF. Catherine Koffman, Regional Director for Africa at the Green Climate Fund, said: “The Southern African Industrial Decarbonization Facility is GCF’s first platform dedicated to decarbonising industrial value chains in Africa. By deploying catalytic first-loss equity where risk is highest, the facility aims to unlock a target $1.2 billion programme across South Africa and Namibia, finance 30 to 40 projects, install about 1.52 GW of renewable energy and avoid an estimated 24.2 million tonnes of emissions. It offers a scalable model for competitive, low-carbon industrial growth.”
Under the GCF-supported programme, CI3 will back green hydrogen, ammonia, methanol and the decarbonisation of hard-to-abate industries. Its catalytic funding absorbs early risk to draw in institutional and commercial investors. Andrew Johnstone, Chief Executive Officer of Climate Fund Managers, said: “CI3 marks an important milestone in Climate Fund Managers’ journey of directing capital, through innovative financing structures, into commercial investments designed to mitigate the causes of climate change and help societies adapt to the consequences we witness every day around us. Decarbonising heavy industry is essential to achieving global climate goals and presents a significant investment opportunity. Yet the scale and complexity of these projects create financing challenges, particularly during development and construction. By helping to mitigate these risks, GCF’s catalytic financing can attract institutional investment into commercially viable projects and support competitive, low-carbon industrial growth.”
CI3’s Development Tranche has initial commitments of EUR 150 million from Invest International and the European Commission. In August 2026, SA-H2 reached a R3 billion (about $182 million) first close. Its backers include the Public Investment Corporation (PIC), Sanlam Life and DBSA. Climate Fund Managers did not disclose CI3’s total raised so far or its final close date.
RELATED ARTICLE: Green Climate Fund Commits $687M to Climate Resilience, Forestry, and Early Warning Projects
Track Record
The approval builds on GCF’s earlier investments in Climate Investor One, Climate Investor Two and the GAIA Climate Loan Fund. It also follows GCF’s accreditation of Climate Fund Managers in July 2026.
Why It Matters
For Climate Fund Managers, the approval adds GCF risk capital to two funds holding six signed development funding agreements. These include Hive Hydrogen’s Coega green ammonia project and HyIron’s Oshivela green iron project. That positions CI3 to carry such projects into construction. If the GCF cover draws more investors like PIC and Sanlam Life, CI3 could reach its $1.2 billion target sooner.

Iberdrola Returns to US Debt Market With $1.6 Billion Green Bond
- Two equal tranches: The $1.6 billion issue is split into two $800 million tranches maturing in 2029 and 2033.
- Strong investor demand: Orders topped $5 billion from 116 investors, more than three times the amount issued.
- US grid and renewables: Proceeds will fund US network assets, mainly transmission, and renewable energy facilities.
Iberdrola has sold $1.6 billion of green bonds in the US debt market, aimed at institutional investors inside and outside the United States. Demand topped $5 billion, more than three times the amount issued, with 116 investors taking part. The proceeds will finance or refinance electricity network assets, mainly transmission, and renewable facilities in the United States.
The issue is split into two tranches of $800 million each. The first matures on November 4, 2029, and carries an annual fixed coupon of 5.40%. The second matures on November 4, 2033, with an annual fixed coupon of 5.85%. Iberdrola said its margins were among the most attractive in the US electricity sector.
Most of the 116 investors were American, including many of the country’s main financial institutions. According to Iberdrola, the bonds’ green status helped increase demand both inside and outside the United States. The company also said the final cost matched what it could have obtained in the Euromarket, reflecting well-chosen timing. Iberdrola did not name the investors or say how proceeds will be split between network and renewable assets.
What’s New
The deal is Iberdrola’s first direct operation in the US market since 2009. Its American subsidiaries have regularly raised money in that market over the same period. Iberdrola said the new channel expands and diversifies its financing sources. It also expects the deal to progressively improve its financing costs in both the US market and the Euromarket.
RELATED ARTICLE: Iberdrola Launches First Carbon Removal Project in Australia
Why It Matters
Iberdrola expects to invest $5 billion a year in the United States in the coming years. The $1.6 billion raise covers part of that need through a funding route that sits alongside its subsidiaries. If demand holds, repeat dollar issues could give it a recurring, lower-cost funding source for its US transmission and renewables build-out.

Climatiq’s ISO 14067 Engine Powers Sweep’s AI Tool for Supplier Product Footprints
- Certified engine: Climatiq’s ISO 14067-certified calculator now runs a guided footprint flow inside Sweep.
- Bill-of-materials input: Suppliers with little or no carbon expertise upload component lists and receive PACT-aligned footprints.
- Single-request campaigns: Buyers can ask each supplier for footprints of everything it supplies at once.
Sweep, the AI-powered sustainability platform, has partnered with Climatiq to help suppliers produce product carbon footprints (PCFs), or per-product emissions estimates. The deal brings Climatiq’s calculation engine, certified to the ISO 14067 product footprint standard, into Sweep’s supply chain offering. Climatiq’s engine draws on emission factors from more than 60 providers across more than 300 regions.
Under the agreement, a supplier uploads a bill of materials, a list of a product’s components. Sweep’s AI and Climatiq’s emission factor matching then fill data gaps and produce a PCF aligned with the PACT methodology. Because every Guided PCF uses one method, buyers can compare footprints and decide where to focus sourcing and reduction. “Climatiq’s mission has always been to put carbon intelligence at the heart of business decision-making. Partnering with Sweep helps us deliver that by making reliable product-level carbon insights accessible across enterprise supply chains at a whole new scale, so that emissions more visible than ever,” said Hessam Lavi, co-founder and CEO of Climatiq.

Through PCF Campaigns, buyers can ask each supplier in a single request for footprints of everything it supplies. Suppliers that already hold PCFs can upload them. The companies did not disclose financial terms, pricing, a launch date or which clients will use Guided PCF. “Heads of sustainability all tell us the same thing: they’d rather have estimated supplier emissions data than supplier-provided data they can’t defend. With Climatiq, we’re giving every supplier, including those starting from scratch, a simple way to produce a credible product footprint, and giving buyers numbers they can actually stand behind in their Scope 3 reporting. This partnership turns a complex, expert-heavy process into a guided AI-driven conversational experience inside Sweep,” said Rachel Delacour, CEO and co-founder of Sweep.
According to the companies, most buyers now accept that spend-based estimates for purchased goods won’t hold up much longer. Yet most suppliers have never calculated a PCF, and their data is often incomplete, inconsistent or impossible to check. California’s SB253 requires large companies operating in the state to report Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions. Meanwhile, Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) obligations are extending to the US subsidiaries of European multinationals.
What’s New for Sweep Buyers
Guided PCF adds a third step to Sweep’s supplier engagement approach. Buyers already use industry-level hotspot estimates to find key suppliers, then supplier-specific enrichment for sharper Scope 3.1 data. Now they can also fund certified PCF calculation for the suppliers where precision matters most.

For Sweep, Guided PCF gives its supply chain offering a certified footprint product that buyers can fund supplier by supplier. For Climatiq, Sweep’s enterprise customers, including L’Oréal, Thales and Crocs, open a channel into their supplier networks. If buyers fund certified footprints at scale, each PCF Campaign could turn one Sweep client into many supplier calculations on Climatiq’s engine.

Clarity AI, a technology platform for extra-financial intelligence, has launched a Transition Credibility Assessment for investors. The tool tests whether companies are making progress toward their climate goals. It measures them against their sector’s decarbonization requirements and the evidence they report.
Clarity AI says climate targets are widespread, but evidence of delivery remains uneven. Its research shows fewer than half of the world’s highest-emitting companies disclose their green capital expenditure (CapEx). articles.title: Who Builds the Systems Green Capabilities Need? – Professor Ioannis Ioannou
articles.summary:
Companies that invest early in green capabilities earn a return only where the infrastructure, markets and rules they depend on are in place, so firms and governments have to build […]
The post Who Builds the Systems Green Capabilities Need? – Professor Ioannis Ioannou appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Who Builds the Systems Green Capabilities Need? – Professor Ioannis Ioannou
Companies that invest early in green capabilities earn a return only where the infrastructure, markets and rules they depend on are in place, so firms and governments have to build those systems together.
Over the past decade, many European companies have built the capabilities a low-carbon economy will need, from capturing carbon at cement plants to making steel with hydrogen and turning old clothes into new fibre. Yet since early 2024, several of the best-known projects have stalled, often after governments had committed money or customers had promised to buy. ArcelorMittal dropped its plans for hydrogen-based steel in Germany in 2025, saying the business case was too weak even with €1.3 billion of public funding on offer. Renewcell, a Swedish pioneer of textile recycling, went bankrupt in 2024. On 22 October, Heidelberg Materials paused a carbon capture project in western Germany that had secured €191 million from the EU. A common reading is that companies are losing their nerve on climate, or that the technologies need more work.
I would argue that in most of these cases the cause lies outside the plant. A company that invests in a capability before the market is ready earns a return only when the systems around it are in place. It needs infrastructure for its plants to connect to, customers willing to pay for what they make, and rules stable enough to recover its investment. Few firms can build such systems on their own. Firms and governments have to build them together, and governments that fund single plants before those systems exist get little for their money.
With my co-author Leandro Nardi, I have been developing an idea we call trapped capabilities. Trapped capabilities are the mirror image of stranded assets: capabilities built over years for an economy that respects environmental and social limits, whose value stays partly locked until the rules, prices and markets around them catch up. The same capability can be trapped in one country and released in another, depending on what governments and other firms have built around it.
Heidelberg Materials, one of the world’s largest cement makers, is pursuing carbon capture across Europe, and three of its projects show the pattern. It already captures carbon at its plant in Brevik, Norway. There, the state expects to pay about two-thirds of a national programme covering the whole chain, from capture to the ships and the storage site under the North Sea. In north Wales, it is building another capture plant under contracts with the British government, which has also backed the pipeline network the plant will use. Germany changed its law in late 2025 to clear the way for carbon pipelines, and who takes on the risk of building them is still an open question. Pipeline companies invest when enough plants sign up, and plants sign up when they are sure the pipeline will come. The EU grant lowers the cost of the Geseke plant, and Heidelberg still runs the risk that the pipeline comes years late. So it has done what a careful investor would do: put its expertise to work first where pipelines and storage exist or have government backing, and hold back where that backing is still missing. By asking Berlin to share that risk with the first companies to commit, it has also told the government which piece of the system it needs.
Beyond heavy industry, companies that recycle and reuse materials run into the same problem, because most of the economy is set up to make, use and throw away. Renewcell built an industrial plant to turn worn-out clothes into pulp for new fibre. It went under after sales fell well behind expectations and fashion brands bought far less recycled fibre than their public commitments had signalled. The EU has since adopted rules that make producers of clothing and other textiles pay to collect, sort and recycle what they sell once people throw it away. National schemes are due by April 2028, more than four years after Renewcell’s collapse. Under a new owner, the plant is due to resume production by the end of this year.
When companies like Heidelberg ask governments to share these risks, they invite a familiar objection: that firms want taxpayers to pay for their own decarbonisation. I think the objection has force when public money goes to one firm’s plant on its own. Pipelines, storage sites and sorting systems are different. They are shared assets, like power grids and ports, worth building when many firms use them and pay for them over time. Under the EU’s textile rules, producers cover that cost. Northern Lights, the storage venture that serves Heidelberg’s Norwegian plant, was built with Norwegian public support. It now has contracts with companies in the Netherlands, Denmark and Sweden, so public money helped build an asset that its customers pay to use.
Boards should count the infrastructure, markets and rules a capability depends on as part of the investment. Before committing to a capability ahead of the market, they should ask who will lay the infrastructure, create the markets and set the rules it needs, and what part their own company will play. They can then use the capability first where those systems exist, join the firms and governments building them, and say publicly which pieces are missing, as Heidelberg has done. Governments, for their part, should put public money first into the pipelines, storage sites and collection systems that many firms will share, and recover the cost from those firms over time.
Many European companies have built capabilities like Heidelberg’s, and much of the value of that expertise depends on systems that are still under construction or yet to be planned. At Geseke, the capability will remain trapped until the German government and the country’s industrial emitters agree who builds and pays for the first pipelines. For as long as that question is open, German companies have good reason to put their expertise to work in countries that have already settled it.
Professor Ioannis Ioannou is a world-renowned expert in sustainability leadership, corporate responsibility, and ESG integration. His award-winning research on strategic sustainability integration and focus on investment markets has established him as a leading voice in the field. An influential educator, Professor Ioannou designed and delivered a six-week online course on Sustainability Leadership and Corporate Responsibility that has enrolled over 1000 senior leaders and board members worldwide.

articles.full_text:
SeABank Splits New Sustainable Finance Framework Across Green, Blue and Social Projects
- Allocation split: SeABank expects to allocate 40-45% to green, 10-15% to blue and 40-45% to social projects.
- External review: S&P Global Ratings issued a Second-Party Opinion on the framework on September 24, 2026.
- Eligibility threshold: Projects must show at least a 20% improvement in energy savings, emissions or water use.
Southeast Asia Commercial Joint Stock Bank (SeABank, HOSE: SSB) has published a Sustainable Finance Framework to guide its sustainable funding. The framework received a Second-Party Opinion, an independent alignment review, from S&P Global Ratings on September 24, 2026. Expected allocations are 40-45% to 14 green categories, 10-15% to 7 blue categories and 40-45% to 5 social objectives.
The framework follows six principles and guidelines from bond and loan market bodies ICMA, LMA, APLMA and LSTA, and from IFC. Eligible projects must meet quantitative criteria, such as a minimum 20% improvement in energy savings, emissions or water use. Every credit application is also screened through SeABank’s Environmental and Social Management System. That system’s exclusion list covers activities related to fossil fuels, coal and deforestation, among others.
By 2030, SeABank targets a 10% cut in greenhouse gas emissions against a baseline year. It also aims to widen financial access for vulnerable groups, women-owned businesses and micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. However, SeABank did not disclose the baseline year, interim milestones or the size of planned funding under the framework.
What’s New
S&P Global Ratings rated SeABank’s 2025 Green and Blue Bond Framework Medium Green, the second-highest on its six-level Shades of Green scale. The new framework builds on those green criteria and adds lending and social categories in one structure. Meanwhile, SeABank has raised nearly US$1.1 billion from lenders including IFC, AIIB, Norfund, Proparco, FMO and DFC. “For SeABank, sustainable development is a guiding principle that runs throughout our development strategy. The Sustainable Finance Framework marks a step forward on this journey, creating a unified foundation for us to mobilize and allocate capital, accompany our customers through their transition, and pursue lasting sustainable value for the economy and the community,” said Nguyen Tuan Anh, Deputy CEO of SeABank.
RELATED ARTICLE: IFC Supports SeABank with $150M to Launch Vietnam’s First Blue Bond, Advancing Climate Finance
Why It Matters
The framework gives SeABank an S&P-reviewed basis for funding its green credit book, which grew more than 150% since end-2025. That book exceeded VND4.1 trillion at end-September, against a 2030 goal of green credit at 5% of total outstanding loans. If enough borrowers meet the 20% thresholds, SeABank could channel more labeled funding from its international lenders into green loans toward that goal.

articles.full_text:
TPG Closes Two Climate Funds With $10.4 Billion Combined
- Final close: TPG closed Rise Climate II and the Global South Initiative with $10.4 billion across the two funds and related vehicles.
- Global South target met: The Global South Initiative reached its $2.5 billion commitment target at final close.
- New investor base: Investors new to TPG supplied 31% of total commitments.
TPG, the global alternative asset manager, has held a final close for Rise Climate II and its Global South Initiative. The two climate strategies and related vehicles drew $10.4 billion in aggregate commitments. Jon Winkelried, Chief Executive Officer of TPG, disclosed the close on the firm’s third-quarter 2026 earnings call.
TPG launched the Global South Initiative at the COP28 climate conference in December 2023. The strategy seeks long-term private equity capital for climate solutions in Global South emerging markets. Its initial commitments included $500 million from ALTÉRRA, a UAE-backed climate investment platform, plus capital from Rise Climate II. At final close, it reached its $2.5 billion target.
Rise Climate invests from growth equity to value-added infrastructure across three themes. These are clean electrons, such as renewables and grids; clean molecules and materials, such as sustainable fuels; and negative emissions, including carbon removal. Investors new to TPG supplied 31% of commitments, but TPG named no investors beyond ALTÉRRA and gave no separate Rise Climate II target. “Our clients recognize the powerful secular trends of rising power demand, the reindustrialization of major economies, and the reshaping of global supply chains, which together are driving an unprecedented need for capital. Our climate franchise is well-positioned to meet that need and build on the momentum within our portfolio,” said Winkelried.
The close came as TPG raised more than $15 billion in the third quarter, bringing its year-to-date total to nearly $42 billion. Private equity accounted for $8.5 billion of the quarter. Gary Stein, Head of Investor Relations at TPG, opened the call alongside Axel André, Chief Financial Officer. Jim Coulter, Executive Chairman and Co-Founder, and Jack Weingart, CEO of TPG Global Wealth Solutions, joined for questions.
Rise Climate Track Record
TPG closed its inaugural Rise Climate fund in 2022 at $7.3 billion, then launched Rise Climate II in 2023. “This highly successful outcome represents a 44% increase over our inaugural fund and further validates TPG’s leadership in the climate sector,” said Winkelried.

Why It Matters
The close gives TPG $10.4 billion to deploy across both developed and Global South climate markets. It also brings TPG first-time relationships with the investors behind 31% of commitments. That opens a path to place those new clients in TPG’s other private equity raises, if the climate portfolios perform.

- Certificate volume: Meta will buy environmental attribute certificates tied to about 200,000 tons of Fortera low-carbon cement over several years.
- Missouri plant: The agreement will support development of the Fortera Cement Plant in Ste. Genevieve, Missouri.
- Expansion options: Meta can use the cement in its own building projects and expand the deal’s volume and duration later.
Fortera, a low-carbon cement manufacturer, has signed a multi-year deal to supply Meta with environmental attribute certificates (EACs), which are tradable claims to a product’s lower-emissions benefit. The certificates are tied to about 200,000 tons of Fortera low-carbon cement. Fortera says the deal gives it long-term revenue visibility to help secure financing for new production facilities. The agreement will support development of the Fortera Cement Plant in Ste. Genevieve, Missouri.
Companies buy EACs to build demand for lower-carbon materials, address supply chain emissions and help finance early-stage manufacturing. Under the deal, Meta may also use the cement in its own building projects. It also holds an option to expand the volume and duration of the partnership in later years. “This agreement marks an important first step in Fortera and Meta’s relationship, and we’re excited by Meta’s efforts to advance plants in our pipeline so we can produce low-carbon cement in more markets where they are building,” said Ryan Gilliam, CEO of Fortera. “Agreements of this scale and duration are what unlock financing and move projects from plans to production. They also show the market that low-carbon cement is a product that buyers are serious about and planning around for years to come.”

Fortera’s ReAct Cement is made using captured CO2 and with 70% fewer emissions than ordinary Portland cement production. The product has been extensively third-party tested and conforms to ASTM standards for use in concrete. “Using waste CO₂ as a primary feedstock turns cement decarbonization into a new economic engine for the United States,” said Gilliam. “We’re bringing a new technology to enable communities with economies built around cement and lime production to remain strong as the industry decarbonizes.”
RELATED ARTICLE: Meta, Rockefeller and Sylvera Back Brazil Carbon Data Project
The Ste. Genevieve site sits along the Mississippi River in the Central Midwest, with transport links for distribution across the U.S. and international markets. Fortera says the project will strengthen domestic cement capacity and reduce reliance on imports, which account for 21% of U.S. cement consumption, according to the 2025 U.S. Geological Survey. The companies did not disclose financial terms, the deal’s exact length, or the plant’s investment amount and construction timeline. “A multi-year commitment is what gets a cement plant financed,” said Devon Lake, Head of Net Zero Strategy, Meta. “Our agreement helps Fortera move the Ste. Genevieve plant from plan to production, which means construction jobs and long-term manufacturing jobs in Missouri, and low-carbon cement available to builders well beyond Meta.”
Why It Matters
For Fortera, Meta becomes a multi-year anchor buyer for a plant that is still moving from plan to production. For Meta, the deal links its demand for low-carbon cement to new domestic supply in markets where it is building. If the agreement helps Fortera close financing for Ste. Genevieve, the plant could become a direct cement source for Meta’s own construction projects, with room to scale through the expansion option.

HASI Lends Terradot $34 Million to Fund Rock Weathering Projects in US, Brazil
- Term loan size: HASI closed a $34 million senior secured term loan for Terradot’s carbon removal projects in the US and Brazil.
- Frontier offtake backing: Fixed-price, multi-year offtake agreements with buyer coalition Frontier support the projects.
- Delivery insurance: CFC provides carbon delivery insurance on the investment, arranged through Marsh.
HA Sustainable Infrastructure Capital (HASI) has closed a $34 million senior secured term loan to carbon removal company Terradot. The loan funds Terradot’s enhanced rock weathering (ERW) projects in the US and Brazil. ERW spreads crushed rock on farmland to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. The companies describe the deal as the largest disclosed debt financing for ERW.
The projects are backed by fixed-price, multi-year offtake agreements with Frontier. An offtake agreement is a contract to buy a project’s future output, here carbon removal. Frontier is a coalition whose members include Google, Salesforce, JPMorgan, Shopify and Stripe, among others. “Terradot’s debt financing demonstrates how long-term purchases together with capital markets can support carbon removal deployment,” said Hannah Bebbington Valori, Head of Frontier. “By providing predictable demand through large, multi-year offtake agreements, Frontier aims to help companies like Terradot secure the capital they need to build and scale.”

The investment is also supported by carbon delivery insurance from CFC, arranged through Marsh. However, the companies did not disclose the loan’s interest rate, its maturity or the Frontier contract volumes. “Lenders only back what they can predict,” said Julia Sekula, CFO and Co-Founder of Terradot. “With contracted demand and years of field data that let us bound risks and forecast delivery, this investment marks an important step in bringing project capital to enhanced rock weathering and building the operating record for larger deployments.”
Under the ERW process, the rock stores captured carbon dioxide for thousands of years while improving soil health for growers. Terradot is scheduled to deploy 1 million tonnes of rock across 60,000 hectares (150,000 acres) of farmland. That deployment spans both countries over the course of 2026 and 2027. “HASI is pleased to partner with Terradot on this investment,” said Annmarie Reynolds, Co-Chief Investment Officer at HASI. “Terradot combines contracted demand, rigorous field data, a repeatable deployment model, and a thoughtful approach to risk, all qualities we look for in every investment.”

According to the companies, it is the largest disclosed ERW debt deal, giving other developers a reference point for project finance. - Credit purchase: Salesforce will buy 500,000 methane reduction credits from Mitti Labs by 2030 under a five-year agreement.

Salesforce has signed a five-year agreement to buy 500,000 high-integrity methane reduction credits from Mitti Labs by 2030. The deal will scale climate-smart rice farming across tens of thousands of smallholder farms in India. The companies did not disclose the price or total value of the agreement.
Climate-smart rice farming replaces continuous flooding with alternate irrigation, letting fields dry out during safe windows. Mitti Labs says the shift can cut methane by up to 50% and water use by up to 40% without affecting yields. By 2030, the partnership is projected to save 700 billion liters of water, about 18 months of Bengaluru’s supply. “Salesforce is a founding member of the Beyond Alliance’s Superpollutant Action Initiative. We know that superpollutant reduction is one of the best ways to slow near-term warming, and we are committed to directing capital toward high-impact mitigation efforts. Reducing methane emissions from rice farming is a scalable climate solution that also helps preserve water resources for future generations,” said Jamila Yamani, PhD, Director of Climate & Energy at Salesforce.

Every credit under the Salesforce agreement will be backed by field-level evidence and satellite-verified field dry-downs. That approach also earned Mitti Labs A ratings from Sylvera in July 2026 and BeZero in October. “Carbon credit buyers are increasingly asking not just what impact a project delivers, but how they can see it for themselves. Having Salesforce join Google in backing rice methane reductions shows that high-integrity, data-verified agricultural credits are becoming a core part of serious climate offsetting strategies. This agreement lets us reach tens of thousands more farmers with practices that cut emissions, save water and strengthen livelihoods,” said Xavier Laguarta, Co-founder at Mitti Labs.

Salesforce is the second global technology company to back Mitti Labs within weeks, after a multi-year partnership with Google. Its commitment joins a partner base that also includes Cool Effect, Ebro Foods and Syngenta. To meet that demand, Mitti Labs plans to issue 2 million credits a year by 2028 from projects in India and Southeast Asia.
